newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Generale Bank independent for now, open to alliance.
newsitem.headline: Generale Bank independent for now, open to alliance.

text.p: Generale Bank, Belgium's biggest bank, said on Tuesday that it was to remain independent for now, but added that it was not against an alliance with a partner, notably fellow Belgian bank Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL).

"We have a stand-alone policy for now, but we are receptive to the message that a bigger Belgian bank would be a good thing," Generale Bank chief executive officer Ferdinand Chaffart said in reply to questions at a news conference about the bank's 1996 earnings.

Asked about comments from Generale Bank shareholder Ste Generale de Belgique (SGB), which has said it was interested in a merger between Generale Bank and BBL, Chaffart said: "The ideal partner does not exist, one has to look at what the opportunities are. But this could be a beautiful opportunity."
Asked whether a merger with BBL would not lead to a social bloodbath, whereby the merged bank would cut jobs and branch outlets, Chaffart said:
"I think it would be possible to do this in a controlled manner, without much pain."

Chaffart's apparent interest in an alliance contrasts sharply with the independent stance he took last year around the same time, when Generale Bank and BBL shareholders also indicated that they favoured a merger. Chaffart, however, stressed that he had not changed his mind.

Generale Bank shares rose five percent on Monday and two percent on Tuesday to close at 14,025 francs, after SGB chief executive Philippe Liotier was quoted as saying that "We are interested in a merger between Generale Bank and BBL, but not at any cost." Liotier's comments, which dated from the end of January, appeared in an investment club magazine interview.

Liotier said that a Generale Bank-BBL merger was blocked by Dutch Internationale Nederlanden Groep (ING), which controls 20 percent of BBL stock and wants to keep a 20 percent stake in a new merged entity. Liotier said this was unacceptable.
A Generale Bank source told Reuters on Tuesday that ING could not block a merger with its 20 percent stake, as a 25 percent stake was needed for a blocking minority.
The source added that ING would have a stake of about eight percent in a new merged entity, which would give it a right to representation on its board. "That is unacceptable for us."
Last week BBL chief executive officer Michel Tilmant also said he saw the future of his bank in a "stand alone" perspective, though he said he would not be against an alliance.
ING so far has refused all comment on its Belgian unit.
